h: Grand stairs, a famous tumble and the best of Cambridge
p: The Fitzwilliam's Founder's Building was designed by George Basevi and is one of the finest neoclassical buildings in the country. Inside, the entrance hall is a riot of marble, columns and gilding, and the sweeping staircase makes everyone feel a little bit grand on their way up to the galleries.

Those stairs have a famous story attached. In 2006 a visitor tripped on his shoelace and tumbled into three Chinese Qing dynasty vases, smashing them into pieces. The museum's conservators painstakingly put them back together, and the tale has become part of museum folklore. Keep your laces tied.

Allow an hour or two for a solid look round, more if you're a real art lover. Because entry is free, it's perfect to pop into between other Cambridge sights, or as a dry refuge if the weather turns. Check what exhibitions are on, as they bring something fresh to each visit.

Trumpington Street is lined with old colleges, and you'll notice the little open water channels running alongside the pavements. They're part of Hobson's Conduit, a 17th-century scheme to bring clean water into the town, so watch your step.

From here the best of Cambridge is all within walking distance. Head into the centre for King's College Chapel and its famous fan-vaulted ceiling, or go down to the river to hire a punt or take a guided punting trip along the Backs past the colleges. Walk the other way down Trumpington Street and you'll reach the University Botanic Garden, a lovely spot for a quiet wander, while Kettle's Yard offers a very different, more intimate kind of art experience.
